rationale: UCR math205C notes, Countability axioms section, define verbatim: 'second countable (or to satisfy the second countability axiom) if there is a countable base for the topology (i.e., a countable family B of open sets such that every open set is a union of sets in B)'. The item is that clause, with the library's standing convention that 'countable' means 'at most countable' (def-countable) made explicit. Same hypotheses, quantifiers and direction. Definition, so no proof component.

UCR notes define verbatim: 'separable if it has a countable dense subset'. The item adds the equivalent form 'every nonempty open subset meets D', which def-dense-top already proves equivalent, so no content is added. Definition, no proof component.

Wikipedia 'Countable chain condition', topology section, gives the same condition on the poset of nonempty open sets; Fremlin 5A4A(d) plus its closing Remark reach it as c(X) <= omega with c(X) = sup{#(G) : G subset of T\{empty} is disjoint}. The item states it directly as 'every pairwise-disjoint family of nonempty open subsets is at most countable' rather than through a cardinal function or an antichain in a poset, which is a reformulation, not a change of content. Convention delta: the library says 'at most countable' where the sources say 'countable'. NOTE the cited UCR notes contain no occurrence of 'countable chain condition' or 'ccc' at all — see finding N1.

Fremlin, Measure Theory vol. 5, 5A4A states each clause verbatim: (a) 'The weight of X, w(X), is the least cardinal of any base for T'; (c) 'The density d(X) of X is the smallest cardinal of any dense subset of X'; (h)(i) 'the character of x in X, chi(x,X), is the smallest cardinal of any base of neighbourhoods of x' and (ii) 'The character of X is chi(X) = sup_x chi(x,X)'. Critically, Fremlin uses the SAME raw convention the item insists on: no aleph_0 normalisation, so a one-member local base has character 1. The item is ai-altered rather than literature-derived only because it merges four separate numbered definitions into one item and adds the explicit no-normalisation paragraph and the justified_by forward pointers; every individual clause is exact. Definition, no proof component.

Fremlin 5A4A(g)(i) states verbatim 'The Lindelof number L(X) is the least cardinal kappa such that every open cover of X has a subcover with cardinal at most kappa', and 5A4A(d) 'The cellularity of X is c(X) = sup{#(G) : G subset of T\{empty} is disjoint}'. Both are exact, including the raw convention. ai-altered because the item merges the two definitions and renames Fremlin's 'Lindelof number' to 'Lindelof degree'; L(X) is unchanged in content. Definition, no proof component.

Fremlin 5A4A closing Remark is an exact source for all five equivalences at once: "Recall that X is called 'second-countable' iff w(X) <= omega, 'separable' iff d(X) <= omega, 'ccc' iff c(X) <= omega ..., 'Lindelof' if L(X) <= omega, ... and 'first-countable' if chi(X) <= omega". Same five properties, same threshold, same direction, and the same raw cardinal functions. Local proof is a library rewrite unfolding each definition, hence ai-generated.

The claim that a countable neighbourhood base may be taken open and nested/decreasing is standard and is stated on Wikipedia 'First-countable space'; the library's own def-first-countable-top records it in its remarks. ai-altered because the item states it as a proposition with a specific construction (interiors, then finite intersections) and because it is written to be explicitly choice-free, which the sources do not remark on. Local proof is a library construction, hence ai-generated.

UCR notes state it in as many words: 'We also know that second countable implies first countable.' Same hypothesis, same conclusion, no choice needed on either side. Local two-step proof (the subfamily of basis members containing x) is the standard argument rewritten in library format, hence ai-generated.

UCR THEOREM 1 states 'A topological space that is second countable is also separable and Lindelof'. The mathematical content is identical. ai-altered for one deliberate refinement the source does not make: the library states the hypothesis AC_omega explicitly in the title and Statement, and spends it at exactly one step (selecting a point from each nonempty basis member). The source works in ZFC and does not track the cost. Local proof ai-generated.

nLab 'second-countable spaces are Lindelof' and UCR THEOREM 1 both state exactly this implication; nLab additionally discusses the choice principle involved. ai-altered for the same reason as its separability twin: the library pins the hypothesis to AC_omega and spends it at one named step (choosing U_B for each eligible basis member). Local proof ai-generated.

UCR THEOREM 1 second half plus its closing sentence 'In particular, all three concepts are equivalent for metric spaces' is the same three-way equivalence for metrizable spaces. ai-altered because the library states it for metrizable (not metric) spaces, packages it as a single iff-iff, and declares AC_omega, spending it in the Lindelof-implies-separable direction only. The 1/n-ball basis and the 2/n < epsilon estimate are the standard arguments in library format; proof ai-generated.

UCR PROPOSITION 2 states verbatim 'A subspace of a second countable space is second countable' (attributed there to Munkres Theorem 30.2). Same hypothesis, same conclusion, no choice. Local proof (traces of basis members) is the standard one-line argument, ai-generated as written.

Wikipedia 'Second-countable space' states that a countable product of second-countable spaces is second countable. UCR PROPOSITION 2 gives only the FINITE product, so the countable case needs the Wikipedia clause. ai-altered because the library states AC_omega explicitly (choosing one basis per factor) and carries out the counting of finite-support boxes from thm-product-of-countable and thm-countable-union-of-countable rather than asserting it. Proof ai-generated.

Wikipedia 'First-countable space' records that a countable product of first-countable spaces is first countable. ai-altered for the explicit AC_omega hypothesis and the in-library counting of finite-support neighbourhood products. Proof ai-generated.

Fremlin 5A4B(a) states c(X) <= d(X), which with 5A4A's Remark ('separable' iff d(X) <= omega, 'ccc' iff c(X) <= omega) is exactly 'separable implies ccc'. ai-altered because the item states the implication directly between the two named properties rather than as a cardinal inequality, and because its proof is written to avoid choice: it enumerates the countable dense set once and takes the FIRST enumerated point of D meeting each U, instead of choosing a point per member. That choice-freeness is a genuine library refinement. Proof ai-generated. NOTE the cited UCR notes never mention ccc - see finding N1.

ESCALATED TO ALPHA. Fremlin 5A4B(a) is an exact source for three of the four asserted inequalities: 'c(X) <= d(X) <= pi(X) <= w(X)' gives c(X) <= d(X) <= w(X), and 't(X) <= chi(X) <= w(X)' gives chi(X) <= w(X). The fourth, L(X) <= w(X), is NOT in 5A4B(a) and I did not locate it anywhere in 5A4; it is standard (a basis of size w(X) refines any open cover) and the item discharges it inline at step 1.3. Because the item merges a sourced trio with one clause I could not source in the cited text, the statement is ai-altered rather than literature-derived. Proof ai-generated.

Fremlin 5A4B(b) states verbatim 'If Y is a subspace of X, then w(Y) <= w(X), t(Y) <= t(X), nw(Y) <= nw(X) and chi(y,Y) <= chi(y,X) for every y in Y'. The item asserts exactly the w and chi clauses of that list, with the same quantifier on y and the same direction; selecting a sublist of a stated conjunction is a cosmetic restriction, not a semantic change. Proof ai-generated.

Fremlin 5A4B(c) states verbatim 'If a topological space Y is a continuous image of X, then d(Y) <= d(X), c(Y) <= c(X), t(Y) <= t(X), L(Y) <= L(X) and nw(Y) <= nw(X)'. The item asserts the d and L clauses of that list under the same hypothesis (continuous surjection), same direction. Proof ai-generated.

Fremlin 5A4B(h) reads 'Suppose that X is metrizable. (i) d(X) = w(X)'. That is the item's Statement exactly, including the raw convention that makes the finite case meaningful. The item's own proof handles infinite and finite density separately, the finite branch showing X = D is finite discrete with w = |X| = d; Fremlin does not split cases, so the proof is ai-generated.

Wikipedia 'Delta-system lemma' states the classical result: every uncountable collection of finite sets contains an uncountable Delta-system (sunflower). Same hypothesis (uncountable family of finite sets), same conclusion (uncountable Delta-subfamily), same direction. The local proof is the standard one - layer by cardinality, induct on n, split on whether some point lies in uncountably many members, Zorn for a maximal disjoint subfamily - rewritten in library format with the choice principles named, hence ai-generated. NOTE the cited UCR notes contain no Delta-system material - see finding N1.

That every Cantor cube 2^I satisfies ccc is standard (Marczewski: any product of separable spaces is ccc) and is recorded on Wikipedia 'Cantor cube'. ai-altered because the library proves the special case directly from its own Delta-system lemma rather than via the general product theorem, and states the choice hypothesis. The claim itself is unchanged. Proof ai-generated. NOTE UCR carries no Cantor-cube or ccc material - see finding N1.

This one IS carried by the cited UCR notes: their 'THE LINDELOF PROPERTY DOES NOT IMPLY SEPARABILITY' example takes X = {0,1}^A with |A| > 2^aleph_0 and proves X is not separable. Same hypothesis and same conclusion. It is the converse half of the Hewitt-Marczewski-Pondiczery theorem. ai-altered because UCR argues by counting continuous real-valued functions on a separable space, whereas the item argues by columns c_i(n) = s(n)(i) and a two-coordinate cylinder; the statement is identical, the route is not. Proof ai-generated.

The refuted claim 'every ccc space is separable' and its standard refutation by a large Cantor cube are textbook (the ccc-but-not-separable example is the canonical separation of the two properties). ai-altered: the library assembles the refutation from its own two lemmas rather than transcribing a source's counterexample. The construction being exhibited (2^I with |I| > 2^aleph_0) is not bespoke. Refutation ai-generated.

An uncountable discrete space as the standard first-countable non-second-countable example is recorded on both Wikipedia pages. ai-altered because the library fixes the witness to discrete R specifically and derives uncountability from its own thm-r-uncountable. Refutation ai-generated.

Wikipedia 'Lower limit topology' records that the Sorgenfrey line is separable but not second countable. Same witness, same two properties. ai-altered because the library gives an explicit injection R -> N via the least index n(x) with x in B_n subset [x,x+1), where sources typically assert non-second-countability. Refutation ai-generated. NOTE UCR has no lower-limit material - see finding N1.

Wikipedia 'Sorgenfrey plane' records that it is separable while its antidiagonal is an uncountable discrete subspace, i.e. separability is not hereditary. UCR gestures at the same phenomenon ('One can construct examples of separable topological spaces that have nonseparable subspaces') without constructing it. ai-altered because the library supplies the construction and verifies the isolating rectangle [x,x+1) x [-x,-x+1) explicitly. Refutation ai-generated.

The one-point compactification of an uncountable discrete space (Fort space) as a Lindelof space with a non-Lindelof open subspace is standard; Wikipedia 'Fort space' and 'Alexandroff extension' carry the ingredients. ai-altered because the library assembles the example from its own thm-one-point-compactification-properties and fixes the witness to discrete R. Refutation ai-generated. NOTE UCR has no one-point-compactification material - see finding N1.

Refutation ai-generated.

That second countability survives countable but not arbitrary products, with a large Cantor cube as the witness, is standard and recorded on Wikipedia 'Second-countable space'. ai-altered because the library routes the refutation through its own second-countable-implies-separable theorem and its non-separability lemma rather than counting a basis directly. Refutation ai-generated.

The closed ball {x : ||x - c|| <= r} and sphere {x : ||x - c|| = r} of a centre and positive radius in Euclidean space are given in exactly this form on Wikipedia 'Euclidean space' and 'Sphere', with S^(n-1) the standard notation for the unit sphere in R^n. The item adds only that these sets carry the subspace topology and that the exponent in S^(n-1) is notation rather than a dimension claim, both of which are bookkeeping, not content. Definition, no proof component.

Wikipedia 'Pseudocompact space' gives the defining condition as: every continuous real-valued function on the space is bounded. That is the item's condition. CONVENTION DELTA, and it is deliberate: many texts reserve 'pseudocompact' for completely regular (or Tychonoff) spaces, and the item explicitly declines that restriction in its own Remark, naming exactly the bounded-image condition. Flagged for Alpha because the choice is library-wide, not local: cex-pseudocompact-noncompact-particular-point-space depends on it, its witness being a non-regular particular-point space. Under the most-widely-adopted rule with Wikipedia as tiebreaker the item's convention is the right one. Definition, no proof component.

That a pseudocompact subset of R^n is bounded is standard and immediate from the source's own definition (the norm is a continuous real-valued function). ai-altered because no located source isolates it as a named lemma; the library splits it out to make the ZF four-way equivalence theorem provable step by step. Proof ai-generated; I checked the empty-set branch, which the item disposes of explicitly.

Companion to the boundedness lemma and standard by the same route (if p is in the closure but not in A, then x -> 1/||x - p|| is continuous and unbounded on A). ai-altered because it is an unnamed step in sources and a named lemma here. Proof ai-generated; I verified the Lipschitz estimate |f(x) - f(a)| <= (2/d^2)||x - a|| on the ball of radius d/2, which is correct.

Every component is exactly sourced - Heine-Borel (compact iff closed and bounded in R^n) and the extreme value theorem - but the four-way equivalence including pseudocompactness, and the explicit assertion that the whole equivalence is a theorem of ZF, is the library's assembly. ai-altered. I verified the ZF claim: thm-heine-borel-rn, thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps clause 2 and both pseudocompactness lemmas are all choice-free, and the cycle 4 => 3 => 2 => 1 => 4 closes. The nonemptiness hypothesis is genuinely needed for condition 4 and the item says so. Proof ai-generated.

That compactness, sequential compactness, countable compactness, limit point compactness, completeness-with-total-boundedness, closed-and-bounded and the extreme value property all coincide for subsets of R^n is standard and recorded on Wikipedia 'Sequentially compact space'. ai-altered because the library states the choice cost precisely - AC_omega and DC, inherited from thm-metric-compactness-equivalences - where sources work in ZFC, and because it grafts the ZF four-way part onto the metric part explicitly. Proof ai-generated.

Compactness of Euclidean closed balls and spheres is the standard immediate corollary of Heine-Borel and is stated on that Wikipedia page for closed balls. ai-altered because the item states balls and spheres together and verifies closedness of each by an explicit radius, using the reverse triangle inequality from lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric. Proof ai-generated.

Wikipedia 'Polygonal chain' defines a polygonal chain as a connected series of straight line segments through a finite vertex list, and polygonal connectedness is the standard derived notion. ai-altered because the item fixes a specific parametrisation on [0,1] by an explicit affine formula on each subinterval of a partition, where sources leave the parametrisation implicit, and because it requires the path to be a path (continuity built into the definition, discharged by the next lemma). Proof ai-generated; I checked that adjacent formulas agree at each shared endpoint t_i, which is what makes the pieces one function.

The clopen-reachable-set argument is the standard engine of the theorem that open connected subsets of R^n are polygonally connected; it appears in sources inside that theorem's proof rather than as a separate statement. ai-altered on that ground: the library isolates it as a lemma about R_a. Proof ai-generated. The step numbering handles the R_a and complement branches in interleaved order but the logic is sound; I checked that a is in R_a via the constant one-segment path, which is what makes R_a nonempty downstream.

Proof ai-generated.

That R^n is connected, path-connected, locally path-connected and locally connected is standard and recorded on Wikipedia 'Euclidean space'. ai-altered because the item states the polygonal strengthening and derives local path-connectedness from convexity of balls. Proof ai-generated.

R^n is the standard example of a locally compact, sigma-compact space and Wikipedia 'Sigma-compact space' names it as such. ai-altered because the item supplies the exhaustion explicitly and shifts the radius to k+1 so that every K_k has POSITIVE radius, which its cited compactness corollary requires; that is a real library-specific adjustment. Proof ai-generated.

Wikipedia 'Countable set' states that a finite product (hence any finite power) of countable sets is countable, with no choice principle needed. Same hypothesis, same conclusion. The item's induction on m from thm-product-of-countable, with C^0 a one-point set, is the standard argument in library format; proof ai-generated.

That Q^n is a countable dense subset of R^n and that rational-endpoint open boxes form a countable basis is standard and recorded on Wikipedia 'Euclidean space' and 'Separable space'. ai-altered because the item is written to be choice-free, routing every coordinatewise selection through lem-finite-choice rather than an unremarked simultaneous choice; that bookkeeping is a genuine library refinement. Proof ai-generated. Cosmetic: frontmatter says proof_strategy direct while the body says constructive - finding N6.

That R^n minus a point is (path-)connected for n >= 2 is standard. ai-altered because the item proves the polygonal strengthening by a specific two-segment construction through a vector z outside span{x} union span{y}, with the existence of z argued by cases (x + y works when the spans differ; otherwise the common span is proper). I verified both cases, including that z is nonzero. Proof ai-generated. Cosmetic: frontmatter proof_strategy direct vs body constructive - finding N6.

I verified the constant: on ||x - a|| < d/2 the two terms each contribute at most ||x - a||/||x||, giving the stated bound 4||x - a||/d. Proof ai-generated.
